question.prompt:
A tetromino consists of four squares connected along their edges. There are five possible tetromino shapes, \(\mathrm{I}\), \(\mathrm{O}\), \(\mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{T}\), and \(\mathrm{S}\), shown below, which can be rotated or flipped over. Three tetrominoes are used to completely cover a \(3 \times 4\) rectangle. At least one of the tiles is an \(\mathrm{S}\) tile. What are the other two tiles?

[Figure 1](figures/2025_AMC_8_Q11_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
An \(\mathrm{S}\) tile occupies either two rows and three columns or three rows and two columns. These two cases cover every rotation and flip. Write the rectangle as three rows of four squares, and use a dot for an uncovered square.

First suppose the \(\mathrm{S}\) occupies two rows. By reflecting the rectangle if necessary, we can put it in the top two rows and the leftmost three columns. There are two possible offsets:
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
S&S&\cdot&\cdot\\
\cdot&S&S&\cdot\\
\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{cccc}
\cdot&S&S&\cdot\\
S&S&\cdot&\cdot\\
\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot
\end{array}.
\]
The second arrangement is impossible: the upper-left square has both of its neighboring squares occupied by \(S\), so no connected tile can cover it.

In the first arrangement, the third square in the top row has only one uncovered neighbor, the upper-right square. These two squares must therefore belong to the same tile. To reach four connected squares, that tile must continue down the rightmost column, forming an \(\mathrm{L}\). The four remaining squares also form an \(\mathrm{L}\). Labeling these two tiles \(X\) and \(Y\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
S&S&X&X\\
Y&S&S&X\\
Y&Y&Y&X
\end{array}.
\]
Now suppose the \(\mathrm{S}\) occupies all three rows. If it uses the leftmost or rightmost pair of columns, an uncovered corner square has both neighbors occupied by \(S\), which is impossible. If it uses the middle two columns, then, up to reflection, the remaining squares split into the following two separate groups:
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
X&X&S&Y\\
X&S&S&Y\\
X&S&Y&Y
\end{array}.
\]
Each group has four squares and forms an \(\mathrm{L}\), so each must be one whole tile.

Thus every possible tiling containing an \(\mathrm{S}\) uses two \(\mathrm{L}\) tiles. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Follow the forced squares

solutions.explanation:
Color the rectangle like a checkerboard. It has six black and six white squares, so the three tiles together must cover equal numbers of the two colors.

Each \(\mathrm{I}\), \(\mathrm{O}\), \(\mathrm{L}\), or \(\mathrm{S}\) can be split into two pairs of edge-adjacent squares. Each pair contains one square of each color, so each of these tiles covers two black and two white squares in every rotation or flip. A \(\mathrm{T}\), however, covers three squares of one color and one of the other. Therefore a single \(\mathrm{T}\) together with two balanced tiles cannot cover the rectangle. This eliminates choices B and E.

Next color entire columns alternately black and white. Again there are six squares of each color. An \(\mathrm{I}\) must be horizontal because the rectangle has only three rows, so it covers two squares of each color. An \(\mathrm{S}\) also always covers two of each: its column counts are either \(1,2,1\) or \(2,2\).

An \(\mathrm{L}\) always covers three squares of one color and one of the other. If its three-square arm is vertical, those three squares share a column color. If that arm is horizontal, its two end squares share a color, and the fourth square has that same color. Thus one \(\mathrm{L}\), together with an \(\mathrm{S}\) and either an \(\mathrm{I}\) or another \(\mathrm{S}\), cannot give equal color totals. This eliminates A and D.

The remaining choice is two \(\mathrm{L}\) tiles, and it works. Here \(X\) and \(Y\) are the two separate \(\mathrm{L}\) tiles:
\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
S&S&X&X\\
Y&S&S&X\\
Y&Y&Y&X
\end{array}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Use two color patterns
